This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 10 - Real-Time Streams and Bots](../../Notebooks/Part%2010%20-%20Real-Time%20Streams%20and%20Bots/Part%2010%20-%20Real-Time%20Streams%20and%20Bots.ipynb).

## Background

> **tl;dr**: Every previous part of this series queried the *past*: we
> asked the API for posts, follows, and likes that already existed.
> ATProto also broadcasts every public event on the network *as it
> happens*. In this part we drink (carefully) from that stream with
> **Jetstream**, do some live analysis of the network's pulse, practice
> data minimization on streaming data, and then close the loop by
> designing a small, polite, clearly-disclosed **bot** that can read and
> write in real time.

### Retrospective search versus streaming

A retrospective design — "search for every post matching X from last
month" — and a streaming design — "capture every post matching X as it
is created" — sound like they should return the same data. They do not:

* **Deletions and survivorship.** A retrospective query only returns
  content that *survived* until the moment you asked: deleted posts,
  deactivated accounts, and blocked or opted-out content have already
  vanished from the index. A stream captures events the moment they
  happen, including the deletion events themselves. Studies of
  contentious topics can look dramatically different depending on which
  design you choose, because deletion is not random. This one-sided
  attrition is called **survivorship bias** — the mistake of generalizing
  from the cases that survived some selection process to all of the
  cases. (The name comes from the World War II statisticians who
  realized that bullet holes on *returning* bombers showed where a plane
  could be hit and still make it home — the fatal hits were on the
  planes nobody got to examine.) A retrospective archive is, by
  construction, a study of survivors.
* **Index completeness.** Search endpoints query an index with its own
  inclusion rules; a **firehose**-style stream — the industry term,
  inherited from Twitter, for a feed of *every* public event a platform
  emits rather than a sampled trickle — is the network's actual event
  log.
* **Sampling transparency.** On Twitter, most researchers could only
  afford the ~1% Streaming API sample, and Morstatter et al. (2013)
  showed that the sample's coverage of topics and hashtags varied wildly
  and non-randomly compared to the full stream. Pfeffer, Mayer &
  Morstatter (2018) later showed the sample could even be deliberately
  *tampered with*. On Bluesky, the full public event stream is free and
  open to everyone — so for once, *you* control the sampling design.

The trade-off: a stream only captures what happens *while you are
listening*. You cannot stream the past. Real research designs therefore
often combine both: a retrospective archive for history, plus a stream
going forward.

### Learning objectives

After completing this document you should be able to:

1. Explain how a streaming collection differs from retrospective search,
   and what deletion/survivorship biases each design has.
2. Connect to **Jetstream** over a websocket, filter events with
   `wantedCollections`, and collect a bounded sample of live network
   events.
3. Read the anatomy of a Jetstream event: `did`, `time_us`, `kind`, and
   the `commit` payload (`operation`, `collection`, `record`).
4. Analyze a live window of activity: the event mix, events-per-second,
   post languages, replies, and media — and extrapolate to network-scale
   daily volumes.
5. Practice **data minimization** on streaming data: store per-second
   aggregates and content-free features instead of raw content.
6. Explain when you need the raw `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`
   firehose instead of Jetstream.
7. Design a minimal, disclosed **reply bot**: poll notifications for
   mentions, build a threaded reply, deduplicate, rate-limit, and
   schedule it.

## Setup

Every API call in Parts 00–09 used HTTP's request–response rhythm: send
one request, receive one response, done. A live stream is different. We
will open a **websocket** — a connection that, after an initial HTTP
handshake, *stays open* so the server can push messages to us
continuously, for minutes or days, without our asking again. The
[websocket](https://rstudio.github.io/websocket/) package provides the
client, and it runs on the [later](https://r-lib.github.io/later/)
package's **event loop**: a scheduler that runs our code whenever a
message arrives. Websocket is the one extra dependency of this part:

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)

has_websocket <- requireNamespace("websocket", quietly = TRUE)
```

As in every part, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks for
credentials and sets `bsky_authed`. This part's gating differs from the
others in one interesting way: **Jetstream requires no authentication
and no client at all** — the live event stream is public infrastructure
— so the streaming chunks are gated on having the websocket package
rather than on credentials. Only the bot sections at the end, which read
notifications and (hypothetically) post, need an account:

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
# Jetstream needs no authentication; bot sections do.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_websocket)
```

## 1. The Jetstream: the network's pulse as friendly JSON

ATProto's source of truth is the **relay firehose**
(`com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`): a websocket on which a relay
re-broadcasts every signed **commit** — every creation, update, or
deletion of a record — from every repository on the network, the
instant it happens. (Recall from Part 00 that each account *is* a
repository of records; a commit is the unit of change to a repository,
in exactly the same sense as a git commit.) The firehose is complete and
cryptographically verifiable — and a chore to consume, because its
messages arrive as binary **CBOR** frames (a compact binary encoding of
JSON-like data) wrapping **CAR** archives (Content Addressable aRchives,
bundles of the records in each commit) that you must decode yourself.
The wire format is specified in the ATProto
[event stream spec](https://atproto.com/specs/event-stream); we return
to the raw firehose in Section 6.

[**Jetstream**](https://bsky.network/blog/jetstream) is an
[open-source service](https://github.com/bluesky-social/jetstream)
operated by Bluesky that does that decoding for you and re-broadcasts
the firehose as plain JSON over a websocket. You give up the
cryptographic verifiability of raw commits, and in exchange you get
events you can `fromJSON()` — which for most monitoring and research
purposes is exactly the right trade. Its query parameters
(`wantedCollections`, `wantedDids`, `cursor`) are documented in the
[Jetstream section of the Bluesky HTTP API reference](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#jetstream/description/introduction).

### Anatomy of a Jetstream event

An **event** is one message on the stream — one JSON object describing
one thing that just happened somewhere on the network. Every event has
three top-level fields plus a payload:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `did` | The account (repository) that produced the event — the actor |
| `time_us` | Event time as microseconds since the Unix epoch |
| `kind` | `commit` (a record was created/updated/deleted), `identity` (handle change), or `account` (status change) |
| `commit.operation` | `create`, `update`, or `delete` |
| `commit.collection` | Which lexicon the record belongs to: `app.bsky.feed.post`, `app.bsky.feed.like`, `app.bsky.graph.follow`, ... |
| `commit.rkey` | The record's key within the collection |
| `commit.record` | The record itself (for creates/updates) — the same shape you have seen all series |

### Server-side filters

The subscribe URL takes query parameters that filter *on the server*, so
you only download what you need:

* `wantedCollections` — repeatable; takes collection **NSIDs**
  (Namespaced Identifiers, ATProto's reversed-domain-name scheme for
  naming record types — `app.bsky.feed.post` is a post,
  `app.bsky.feed.like` a like, `app.bsky.graph.follow` a follow; see the
  [NSID spec](https://atproto.com/specs/nsid)). Trailing wildcards like
  `app.bsky.graph.*` work too. No filter = everything.
* `wantedDids` — repeatable, up to 10,000 DIDs; restricts the stream to
  specific accounts. This is how you would monitor a *panel* of accounts
  in real time.

`build_jetstream_url()` composes that URL from a vector of collections
(and, optionally, DIDs):

```{r jetstream-url}
JETSTREAM_URL <- "wss://jetstream2.us-east.bsky.network/subscribe"

WANTED_COLLECTIONS <- c(
  "app.bsky.feed.post",     # posts (and replies and quotes)
  "app.bsky.feed.like",     # likes
  "app.bsky.graph.follow"   # follows
)

build_jetstream_url <- function(collections, dids = NULL) {
  params <- c(paste0("wantedCollections=", collections),
              if (length(dids)) paste0("wantedDids=", dids))
  paste0(JETSTREAM_URL, "?", paste(params, collapse = "&"))
}

build_jetstream_url(WANTED_COLLECTIONS)
```

## 2. Collecting a live sample

Now we listen for about a minute. The collector is bounded **twice** — by
wall-clock duration *and* by a maximum event count — because the one
cardinal rule of streams is that they never end on their own. An
unbounded collector is how you fill your laptop's memory by accident.

Websockets are event-driven, so the code reads differently from
everything else in this series. We register an `onMessage` callback that
fires once per arriving event, and then run a small loop that hands
control to the event loop (`later::run_now()`) until the deadline. The
`<<-` assignments let the callback update the shared `events` list that
lives outside it. The chunk takes a full minute to run *by design*.

For reproducibility we record *when* we collected and with what
parameters — with streaming data, the collection window **is** the
dataset definition. A minute of Bluesky at European lunchtime and a
minute during a US election debate are different worlds:

```{r collect}
DURATION_SECONDS <- 60     # how long to listen
MAX_EVENTS <- 20000        # hard safety cap

collect_events <- function(duration_seconds = DURATION_SECONDS,
                           max_events = MAX_EVENTS,
                           collections = WANTED_COLLECTIONS, dids = NULL) {
  events <- vector("list", max_events)
  n <- 0
  done <- FALSE
  ws <- websocket::WebSocket$new(build_jetstream_url(collections, dids),
                                 autoConnect = FALSE)
  ws$onMessage(function(event) {
    if (n >= max_events) {
      done <<- TRUE
      return()
    }
    n <<- n + 1
    events[[n]] <<- fromJSON(event$data, simplifyVector = FALSE)
  })
  ws$onClose(function(event) done <<- TRUE)
  ws$connect()
  deadline <- Sys.time() + duration_seconds
  while (!done && Sys.time() < deadline) {
    later::run_now(0.25)
  }
  ws$close()
  later::run_now(0.5)
  compact(events[seq_len(n)])
}

collection_started <- now("UTC")
events <- collect_events()

cat("Collection started", format(collection_started, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S UTC"),
    "and gathered", length(events), "events\n")
```

### How fast is the network moving?

Every event carries `time_us`, its timestamp in **microseconds since the
Unix epoch** (midnight UTC, January 1, 1970 — the standard zero-point for
computer clocks). Subtracting the first event's timestamp from the last
measures our window in *stream time* — by the network's own clock rather
than ours, which sidesteps any lag between an event happening and our
laptop receiving it. Dividing the event count by that window gives the
headline number: how many things per second the whole network is doing,
in just these three collections. Expect several hundred per second at a
typical hour. (If the count above equals `MAX_EVENTS`, the safety cap
stopped the collection before the minute was up — the stream was busier
than the cap allowed.)

```{r rate}
times_us <- map_dbl(events, "time_us")
window_seconds <- (max(times_us) - min(times_us)) / 1e6
events_per_second <- length(events) / window_seconds

c(events = length(events),
  seconds = round(window_seconds, 1),
  events_per_second = round(events_per_second, 1))
```

### Inspecting one event

Let's look at a single freshly-created post event. One habit worth
building from the very first moment of streaming work: **we redact the
post text and truncate the author identifier before even displaying
it.** These are strangers who posted seconds ago with no idea a tutorial
is watching; we need the event's *structure*, not their words (see
Section 5 and the Ethics note). R lists are copied when modified, so
editing `redacted` leaves the original event untouched:

```{r inspect-event}
sample_post <- detect(events, \(e) identical(e$kind, "commit") &&
                        identical(e$commit$operation, "create") &&
                        identical(e$commit$collection, "app.bsky.feed.post"))

redacted <- sample_post
redacted$did <- paste0(substr(redacted$did, 1, 12), "...")
record <- redacted$commit$record
if (!is.null(record$text)) {
  record$text <- sprintf("[%d characters redacted]", nchar(record$text))
}
if (!is.null(record$facets)) record$facets <- "[redacted]"
if (!is.null(record$embed)) record$embed <- list(`$type` = record$embed$`$type`)
if (!is.null(record$reply)) {
  # The parent and root URIs name other people's posts (and their DIDs):
  # keep the structure, drop the identifiers
  record$reply <- map(record$reply, \(ref) list(cid = "[redacted]", uri = "[redacted]"))
}
redacted$commit$record <- record

cat(substr(toJSON(redacted, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE), 1, 1500))
```

Even redacted, the event tells us a lot: who acted (`did`), when
(`time_us`), what kind of action (`commit.operation` +
`commit.collection`), and the record's metadata — its declared language
(`langs`), whether it is a reply (`reply` carries the thread's root and
parent references — redacted above, because they point at other people's
posts — exactly the structure our bot will construct in Section 7), and
whether it embeds media or links (`embed.$type`).

Notice also that some events have `operation: "delete"`. A stream sees
deletions happen — a retrospective search never does. That asymmetry is
the survivorship bias we opened with, made visible.

## 3. What a minute of Bluesky looks like

Let's flatten the events into a tibble. We keep only structural fields —
and we pseudonymize the actor immediately with `hash_did()` (SHA-256 via
the digest package, truncated to 12 characters as in the Python
version), because nothing in this analysis needs to know *who* anyone
is, only that actions by the same account can be grouped.

Be precise about what that buys. Hashing is **pseudonymization, not
anonymization**: DIDs are public, so anyone who suspects a particular
account can hash its DID and look for a match. Treat hashed identifiers
as sensitive whenever the behavior they index is sensitive, and for real
collections mix in a secret *salt* (a private random string prepended
before hashing) so outsiders can't run that check:

```{r flatten}
hash_did <- function(did, length = 12) {
  map_chr(did, \(d) substr(digest::digest(d, algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE), 1, length))
}

events_df <- map(events, \(e) tibble(
  author_hash = hash_did(e$did),
  timestamp = as_datetime(e$time_us / 1e6),
  kind = e$kind %||% NA_character_,
  operation = e$commit$operation %||% NA_character_,
  collection = e$commit$collection %||% NA_character_
)) |> list_rbind()

head(events_df)
```

### The event mix

What does the network actually spend its time doing? On Twitter, likes
outnumbered tweets by a wide margin, and the same is true here: most
events are **likes**, with posts and follows trailing well behind.
Lightweight reactions are the bulk of social media behavior — worth
remembering whenever a study treats *posts* as "the data".

```{r mix}
events_df |>
  count(collection, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3))

count(events_df, operation, sort = TRUE)
```

### Events per second over time

Streaming data is fundamentally a time series. Counting events per
second by collection gives us the network's heartbeat for the window we
observed — and is exactly the kind of *aggregate* we will save to disk
later instead of the raw events.

```{r eps, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
per_second <- events_df |>
  mutate(second = floor_date(timestamp, "second")) |>
  count(second, collection) |>
  # first and last seconds are partial windows
  filter(second > min(second), second < max(second))

ggplot(per_second, aes(second, n, color = collection)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time (UTC)", y = "Events per second",
       title = paste("Live Bluesky events,",
                     format(collection_started, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC"))) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Two things to notice in the figure. First, the **likes** line rides well
above the others the whole way — the event-mix table above, rendered as
a time series. Second, the second-to-second jitter is real and
unavoidable: independent actions by millions of people arrive roughly at
random, so per-second counts fluctuate around the underlying rate
(statisticians model such arrival counts as a Poisson process). This is
why a single second — or a single minute — is a *noisy* estimate of the
network's pace, and why the monitoring designs at the end of this
document insist on long or repeated windows. A sharp spike is not
necessarily news, either: it can be one account or automated service
writing in a burst.

### Post-level features (without the posts)

For the posts specifically, we extract a deliberately minimal,
**content-free** feature set from each newly created post: a
pseudonymous author hash, the timestamp, the declared language, whether
it is a reply, and whether it embeds media. No text. We can answer real
questions about the live network — *what share of posting is
conversation? what languages is the network speaking right now?* —
without storing a single word anyone wrote:

```{r post-features}
posts_live <- map(events, \(e) {
  commit <- e$commit
  if (is.null(commit) || commit$operation != "create" ||
      commit$collection != "app.bsky.feed.post") {
    return(NULL)
  }
  record <- commit$record
  tibble(
    author_hash = hash_did(e$did),
    timestamp = as_datetime(e$time_us / 1e6),
    lang = unlist(record$langs)[1] %||% NA_character_,
    is_reply = !is.null(record$reply),
    has_embed = !is.null(record$embed),
    has_image = identical(record$embed$`$type`, "app.bsky.embed.images")
  )
}) |> list_rbind()

reply_share <- mean(posts_live$is_reply)
cat(nrow(posts_live), "newly created posts in the window;",
    sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reply_share), "of them are replies to another post\n")

posts_live |>
  summarise(across(c(is_reply, has_embed, has_image), mean))
```

The reply share printed above
(`r if (exists("reply_share")) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reply_share) else "printed when the chunk runs"`
in this knit) is the fraction of new posts that answer another post. It
moves around a lot from one window to the next — a minute dominated by
one busy conversation, or by an automated account posting in a burst,
can push it well above or below the network's long-run average — so a
single minute is a weak estimate (Exercise 4 asks you to see how much it
varies). In every window, though, replies are a large share of new
posts: much of what counts as "posting" is conversation rather than
broadcast. A substantial minority of posts also carry an embed (images,
video, links, or quoted posts).

What languages is the network speaking *right now*? The `langs` field is
self-declared by the posting client, so treat it as a noisy indicator
(Part 06 discusses language identification properly):

```{r langs, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
lang_counts <- posts_live |>
  mutate(lang = replace_na(lang, "(none declared)")) |>
  count(lang, sort = TRUE)

lang_counts |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(lang, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "New posts in window", y = NULL,
       title = "Declared languages of live posts (top 10)") +
  theme_minimal()

cat(sprintf("%.0f%% of posts are in the top-10 languages\n",
            100 * sum(head(lang_counts$n, 10)) / sum(lang_counts$n)))
```

## 4. From one minute to the whole network

A back-of-the-envelope extrapolation: if the network kept this minute's
pace for 24 hours, how many events would that be? (It will not keep this
exact pace — Part 05 showed strong diurnal rhythms, so a single minute
over- or under-shoots depending on when you collect. Treat these as
order-of-magnitude estimates.)

```{r extrapolate}
events_df |>
  count(collection) |>
  mutate(per_second = round(n / window_seconds, 2),
         per_hour = round(per_second * 3600),
         per_day_extrapolated = round(per_second * 86400))
```

### What a 1% sample would mean

For most of Twitter's research era, this back-of-the-envelope ran in the
*other* direction. Researchers got the free "spritzer" Streaming API
(~1% of tweets); the 10% "Decahose" and the full firehose were sold at
prices most academics could not pay. Morstatter et al. (2013) compared
the 1% stream against the firehose and found its coverage of hashtags,
topics, and networks varied day to day and *not* at random — and
Pfeffer, Mayer & Morstatter (2018) demonstrated that the sampling
mechanism could be gamed to inject content into "random" samples.

Here is what a Twitter-style 1% sample of our own window would have
given us:

```{r one-percent}
SAMPLE_RATE <- 0.01

events_df |>
  count(collection, name = "we_observed") |>
  mutate(one_percent_sample_keeps = round(we_observed * SAMPLE_RATE))

cat("A 1% sample of this window would keep about",
    floor(nrow(posts_live) * SAMPLE_RATE),
    "posts -- try estimating a language distribution from that.\n")
```

On Bluesky the full stream is open to anyone, so the census is free and
*sampling is a design choice you make and document yourself* — sample by
time window, by account panel (`wantedDids`), or by random hash of the
DID — rather than an opaque platform decision made for you. That is a
quiet but profound improvement in research infrastructure.

## 5. Data minimization in practice

We just held every event from our window in memory, including the full
text of every post strangers wrote during our window. What should we
*persist*?

The minimization principle from Part 01 applies with extra force to
streams, because streams scale so easily: a document that saves
"everything, just in case" turns into a multi-gigabyte archive of
bystanders' content within hours. Our research questions here needed (1)
event *rates* and (2) content-free post *features*. So that is all we
save:

* **`data/stream_summary.csv`** — per-second event counts by collection.
  Pure aggregate; nobody is identifiable.
* **`data/stream_sample.csv`** — up to 200 post events with a *hashed*
  author identifier, timestamp, language, is-reply, and embed flags.
  **No post text, no URIs, no handles.** We draw them at random with a
  fixed seed, so the sampling step itself is reproducible from the same
  collection.

Everything else is discarded when the R session ends. If a future
question needs more, collect again with the fields that question
requires — the stream will still be flowing. (One more reason to prefer
aggregates: users delete posts, and our saved files should not quietly
resurrect what the network has forgotten.)

```{r minimize}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

per_second |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = collection, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  write_csv("data/stream_summary.csv")

set.seed(42)
posts_live |>
  slice_sample(n = min(200, nrow(posts_live))) |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  write_csv("data/stream_sample.csv")

saved <- c("data/stream_summary.csv", "data/stream_sample.csv")
tibble(file = saved, kilobytes = round(file.size(saved) / 1024, 1))
```

A reproducibility note to keep alongside any streaming archive:
**record the collection window and parameters.** Ours are printed in
this document's output — collection start time, duration, the
`wantedCollections` filter, and the Jetstream instance — which is what
another researcher needs to understand (if not exactly reproduce) a
sample of a stream that never repeats itself.

## 6. The raw firehose: `com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`

Jetstream is a convenience layer *operated by someone else*. The
protocol-native stream is the relay firehose,
`com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`, and sometimes you need it:

* **Full fidelity and verifiability.** The firehose carries the actual
  signed commits, so you can cryptographically verify that events are
  authentic — Jetstream asks you to trust its operator.
* **Everything, not just app.bsky.** New lexicons and non-Bluesky
  applications on ATProto appear in the firehose by definition.
* **Account and identity events** with complete detail, plus the commit
  structure itself (useful for keeping a full mirror of repositories).
* **Independence.** If the Jetstream service changes, rate-limits, or
  disappears, the firehose is the protocol-guaranteed interface.

The cost is decoding: frames arrive as binary CBOR, and the records
inside each commit travel as a CAR file you must unpack. R has no mature
decoder for either, so this document does not consume the firehose. The
Python notebook's Section 6 builds a complete handler (without starting
it) using the atproto SDK's `FirehoseSubscribeReposClient` — about ten
lines of decoding that Jetstream does for us — and the
[event stream spec](https://atproto.com/specs/event-stream) documents
the frame-by-frame wire format. The practical guidance is
language-independent: use Jetstream unless you need verifiability or
collections Jetstream won't filter, and budget for reconnection logic in
anything long-running.

## 7. Building a bot: closing the loop

So far this series has only ever *read*. A **bot** combines reading (a
trigger: a mention, a hashtag, a schedule) with the write endpoints from
Part 00. The smallest responsible design is a **mention-triggered reply
bot**, built from a few composable pieces: poll notifications, keep the
mentions, decide on a reply with a *pure function* (one whose output
depends only on its input, so it can be tested with no network at all),
and send — with deduplication and rate limits around the send.

Because the decision logic is pure, we can exercise the bot's whole
brain right now, unauthenticated:

```{r bot-logic, eval=TRUE}
OPERATOR_PLACEHOLDER <- "@your-handle.bsky.social"

bot_operator <- function() Sys.getenv("BOT_OPERATOR", OPERATOR_PLACEHOLDER)
operator_is_set <- function() {
  op <- bot_operator()
  startsWith(op, "@") && op != OPERATOR_PLACEHOLDER
}
disclosure <- function() {
  paste0("\n\n[I am an automated account: bot run by ", bot_operator(), "]")
}

build_reply <- function(text) {
  if (str_detect(text %||% "", regex("\\bping\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
    paste0("pong! (", format(now("UTC"), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S UTC"), ")", disclosure())
  } else {
    NA_character_   # silence is a feature
  }
}

cat(build_reply("hey @examplebot.bsky.social ping"), "\n---\n")
c(build_reply("lovely weather today"),   # NA: not a command
  build_reply("shipping update"))        # NA: "ping" must be a whole word
cat("Operator named in the disclosure:", bot_operator(), "\n")
```

Three design choices to notice.

**First, the reply discloses that it is a bot — and who runs it.** That
line is appended to every reply, and the same statement belongs in the
bot account's display name and bio. The operator's handle comes from the
`BOT_OPERATOR` environment variable, which is unset above, so the
disclosure shows a placeholder. Set it to *your* handle before running a
real bot (`Sys.setenv(BOT_OPERATOR = "@you.bsky.social")`, or a line in
`~/.Renviron`). Naming the responsible human is what makes a disclosure
useful: it tells people who to contact, and it means your copy of this
bot can never be mistaken for anyone else's.

**Second, the bot ignores everything that is not its one command.** A
bot that replies to everything is indistinguishable from spam.

**Third, "its one command" means the whole *word* "ping".** A simple
substring test would also fire on "shipping", "helping", and "keeping",
and the bot would reply to people who never addressed it. The regular
expression `\\bping\\b` uses word boundaries (`\\b` matches the edge of a
word), so "shipping update" returns `NA`. Small text-matching bugs
become public mistakes once a bot is live, which is why the Python
version of this function has tests
([`tests/test_bot.py`](../../tests/test_bot.py)).

### Threading a reply

A Bluesky reply record carries two *strong references* (URI + CID
pairs): **`parent`** is the post being answered, and **`root`** is the
first post of the thread (Part 04 used this same structure to
reconstruct reply trees). bskyr's
[`bs_post()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_post.html)
builds both for you when you pass the URL of the post you are answering
as its `reply` argument, so the answer lands in the same thread.

### Reading the bot's inbox

Notifications are private to the account, so this — like everything
below — requires authentication. bskyr's
[`bs_get_notifications()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_notifications.html)
wraps `app.bsky.notification.listNotifications`
([API reference](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskynotification/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.notification.listNotifications)).
It is also the gentlest trigger, because people opt in by mentioning
you:

```{r notifications, eval=FALSE}
notifications <- bs_get_notifications(limit = 25)

count(notifications, reason, sort = TRUE)
mentions <- filter(notifications, reason == "mention")
```

### One full cycle, as a dry run

Now the whole loop. A **dry run** is a rehearsal mode: the program
performs every step of the real thing *except the irreversible one*, and
prints what it would have done instead. (The term comes from
command-line tools — `rsync --dry-run` shows which files it would copy
without copying them.) The cycle enforces every safety invariant,
matching the Python version:

* a cap on replies per run, and a pause between sends;
* **a rehearsal changes nothing**: a dry run neither posts nor records
  any mention as answered, so rehearsing never causes the real run to
  skip someone;
* **no operator, no posting**: a live run refuses to post until
  `BOT_OPERATOR` names the human responsible;
* **each send is recorded immediately**: the set of answered mentions is
  saved to disk right after every successful reply, so a failure partway
  through a cycle never causes a double reply.

**This chunk is never executed when knitting** (`eval=FALSE`) — write
actions are deliberate acts:

```{r bot-cycle, eval=FALSE}
MAX_REPLIES_PER_RUN <- 5
SECONDS_BETWEEN_REPLIES <- 5
ANSWERED_FILE <- "data/answered_notifications.json"

save_answered <- function(answered) {
  dir.create(dirname(ANSWERED_FILE), showWarnings = FALSE)
  write_json(as.list(sort(unique(answered))), ANSWERED_FILE)
}

run_bot_once <- function(dry_run = TRUE) {
  if (!dry_run && !operator_is_set()) {
    stop("Refusing to post: set BOT_OPERATOR to the handle of the human ",
         "responsible for this bot, e.g. Sys.setenv(BOT_OPERATOR = \"@you.bsky.social\")")
  }
  answered <- if (file.exists(ANSWERED_FILE))
    unlist(read_json(ANSWERED_FILE)) else character(0)

  mentions <- bs_get_notifications(limit = 25) |>
    filter(reason == "mention", !uri %in% answered) |>
    mutate(text = map_chr(record, "text", .default = "")) |>
    mutate(reply = map_chr(text, build_reply)) |>
    filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
    slice_head(n = MAX_REPLIES_PER_RUN)

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(mentions))) {
    if (dry_run) {
      message("DRY RUN - would reply to ", mentions$uri[[i]],
              ": ", mentions$reply[[i]])
    } else {
      bs_post(text = mentions$reply[[i]],
              reply = bs_uri_to_url(mentions$uri[[i]]))
      answered <- c(answered, mentions$uri[[i]])
      save_answered(answered)          # record each send at once
      Sys.sleep(SECONDS_BETWEEN_REPLIES)
    }
  }
  invisible(nrow(mentions))
}

run_bot_once(dry_run = TRUE)
```

Make this your habit for *any* code that writes to a platform —
rehearse first, read the rehearsal output, then (and only then) go live.

### Scheduling the bot

`run_bot_once()` is deliberately a *single* cycle so that the scheduler
can live outside your code, where it is easiest to reason about. The
classic scheduler is [**cron**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron), the
standard Unix background service that runs commands on a fixed schedule.
You declare your jobs in a **crontab** ("cron table"), one line per job:
a five-field schedule pattern followed by the command to run
([crontab.guru](https://crontab.guru/) decodes the patterns — `* * * * *`
means "every minute", `0 9 * * *` means "09:00 every day"). Save the bot
functions and a final `run_bot_once(dry_run = FALSE)` line in `bot.R`,
then add a crontab entry that runs it every minute, setting the operator
and logging output:

```
* * * * * cd /home/you/pingbot && BOT_OPERATOR=@you.bsky.social Rscript bot.R >> bot.log 2>&1
```

The [cronR](https://cran.r-project.org/package=cronR) package can write
that entry for you from R. Polling once a minute is gentle, debuggable,
and plenty fast for a mention bot — conversation rarely needs streaming
latency.

**Variant: a scheduled posting bot.** Many beloved bots have no trigger
at all — they just post on a schedule (an hourly artwork, a daily
statistic). That is the same pattern minus the notification polling: a
script that checks `bsky_authed` and `operator_is_set()`, then calls
`bs_post()` once with the disclosure appended. For an event-driven bot
(responding to a hashtag the moment it appears), combine this part's two
halves: a Jetstream consumer filtered to `app.bsky.feed.post` that
watches for the trigger and calls the same send logic — with the same
deduplication and rate limiting.

### Write rate limits: the points system

Bluesky PDS hosts meter *writes* with a
[points system](https://bsky.network/blog/rate-limits-pds-v3): a record
**create costs 3 points**, an **update 2**, a **delete 1**, with budgets
of **5,000 points per hour** and **35,000 points per day** per account —
roughly 1,666 creates per hour. Those are hard ceilings for spam
control, not targets: our bot's self-imposed limits (`MAX_REPLIES_PER_RUN
= 5` per cycle, a sleep between sends) keep it orders of magnitude below
them, which is where a research bot belongs. There are also per-IP and
per-session request limits, documented in the
[rate limits guide](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/rate-limits)
(Part 01 covered reading politely with backoff).

### What your bot must never do

Ferrara et al. (2016) chronicle how *social bots* — automated accounts
that imitate humans — polluted Twitter: inflating follower counts,
astroturfing political hashtags, spreading misinformation, and
contaminating a decade of research samples. The norms below are the
difference between a community resource and a pest:

* **Never impersonate a human.** Disclose automation in the bio, display
  name, *and* the posts themselves.
* **Never interact uninvited at scale.** Reply when mentioned, post to
  your own timeline; do not cold-reply to strangers, mass-follow, or
  mass-like.
* **Respect blocks and mutes immediately**, honor deletion, and provide
  a human contact in the bio.
* **Never manufacture consensus** — no coordinated amplification, no
  astroturfing, no engagement farming.
* **Mind the platform's norms**: Bluesky's
  [community guidelines](https://bsky.social/about/support/community-guidelines)
  require labeling automated accounts, and bot accounts that annoy
  people get blocked, reported, and defederated from feeds.

## 8. Research designs with streams

What does real-time access buy a researcher that Parts 01–09 could not?

* **Breaking-event monitoring.** When news breaks, retrospective search
  will later show you the surviving posts; a stream you started
  *beforehand* captures the full arc — including the posts that get
  deleted as the story develops, often the most analytically interesting
  ones. Standing collectors (Jetstream filtered to `app.bsky.feed.post`,
  watching for event keywords) are the streaming analogue of the
  event-study designs in Part 05, and they require you to specify the
  design *before* the data exist — a natural pre-registration.
* **Population-level measurement.** Because the stream is the census,
  base rates are actually computable: posts per day, the reply share,
  language composition, like-to-post ratios. On Twitter, every one of
  those numbers depended on an opaque platform sample that Morstatter et
  al. (2013) showed was biased and Pfeffer, Mayer & Morstatter (2018)
  showed was manipulable. Here you can *compute* the sampling properties
  of any cheaper design (a 1% hash sample, a panel of DIDs) against the
  full stream.
* **Panel designs.** `wantedDids` turns Jetstream into a real-time panel
  study: follow up to 10,000 consented or public-figure accounts and
  observe posting, liking, and following behavior with second-level
  timestamps.
* **Prospective sampling.** Part 04's cascade studies had to select
  posts that were already successful; sampling posts *at birth* from the
  stream dissolves that selection problem.
* **Bots as instruments.** Beyond mischief, disclosed bots have a
  research lineage: field experiments on social contagion and norm
  enforcement used bot accounts as randomized treatments. Any such
  design needs IRB review, disclosure, and debriefing — humans on the
  other end have not consented to be subjects.

## Ethics and limitations

**Bots interact with people who never signed up for a study.** Automated
accounts must disclose that they are automated — in the bio, in the
display name, and in the posts themselves — and should act only when
invited (a mention) or in their own space (their timeline). If a bot is
part of a research design, that design needs informed-consent thinking
and institutional review, not just rate limiting; Ferrara et al. (2016)
document the damage undisclosed bots did to both Twitter's users and
Twitter research.

**Streams make over-collection effortless, so minimize by design.** This
document held thousands of strangers' posts in memory but persisted only
per-second aggregates and a 200-row, content-free, pseudonymized feature
sample. That is the pattern to copy: decide what the research question
needs *before* the collector runs, store aggregates and derived features
rather than content, hash identifiers you do not need, record the
collection window and parameters, and let everything else evaporate with
the session. Remember that hashing is pseudonymization, not
anonymization, and that saved archives should honor deletions the
network has processed since.

**Limitations.** A one-minute window is a snapshot, not an estimate —
diurnal and event-driven variation swamp any single window, so
monitoring designs need long or repeated collections. Jetstream is a
convenience service: it can lag, drop, or change, and it strips the
cryptographic verifiability of raw commits (use `subscribeRepos` when
fidelity matters; reconnect logic and cursor replay matter for
production collectors). Self-declared `langs` labels are noisy. And
Bluesky's population is not "the public": extrapolated daily volumes
describe this network, not social media in general.

## Exercises

1. **A longer window.** Re-run the Section 2 collection with
   `DURATION_SECONDS <- 300` (five minutes). Before running it, use this
   document's events-per-second figure to predict whether the
   `MAX_EVENTS <- 20000` safety cap will cut the collection short — then
   check your prediction against the event count, and raise the cap if
   needed. How much smoother is the per-second plot with five minutes of
   data than with one?
2. **A wider event mix.** Add `app.bsky.feed.repost` and
   `app.bsky.graph.block` to `WANTED_COLLECTIONS` (or use the wildcard
   `app.bsky.graph.*`) and re-collect. How do reposts compare to likes in
   volume? What fraction of graph events are blocks rather than follows?
   Remember that each added collection raises the event rate, so revisit
   your caps.
3. **A real-time panel.** `collect_events()` already accepts a `dids`
   argument and passes it to `build_jetstream_url()`. Resolve a few
   high-traffic accounts to DIDs with
   [`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html)
   (its `did` column) and listen for several minutes. (Quiet panels
   produce few events; pick busy accounts or be patient.)
4. **Two times of day.** Run the one-minute collection at two very
   different local times (say, early morning and mid-evening UTC),
   saving each `per_second` summary to a differently named CSV in
   `data/` along with its collection start time. Compare overall rates,
   the event mix, the reply share, and the language distribution — and
   connect what you find to the diurnal rhythms of Part 05.
5. **Like-to-post ratios across the day.** Using several short windows
   spread across a day (Exercise 4's setup, repeated), estimate the ratio
   of like events to post-creation events per window. Is the ratio more
   stable than the raw volumes? A stable ratio under changing volume
   would suggest the *composition* of activity stays put even as the
   crowd's size breathes.
6. **Watching survivorship happen.** In a fresh collection, compute the
   share of `app.bsky.feed.post` events whose `operation` is `delete`,
   and extrapolate to deletions per day. What does that number imply
   about a retrospective archive collected a month from now — and about
   studies that quietly assume deletion is random?

## Research project ideas

**1. A pre-registered breaking-event monitor.** *Question:* how do
posting volume, reply share, language mix, and — crucially — deletion
rates change around a scheduled public event (an election debate, a
championship final, a major product launch)? *Data:* a standing
Jetstream collector filtered to `app.bsky.feed.post`, started hours
before the event and run through the day after, persisting only
per-minute aggregates and content-free post features (this part's
minimization pattern), plus identical collections on comparison days for
a baseline. *Method:* the interrupted time-series designs from Part 05,
applied to the per-minute series; because the collector must be
specified before the event happens, the design is naturally
pre-registerable. *Expected challenge:* collector reliability — a laptop
that sleeps, a dropped websocket, or a missing reconnect-and-resume loop
produces gaps that look exactly like effects, so production collectors
need supervision, logging, and Jetstream's cursor-replay support.

**2. How good is a cheap sample? A Morstatter-style audit on an open
firehose.** *Question:* which sampling designs — a 1% sample by hash of
DID, fixed time slices, an account panel via `wantedDids` — faithfully
reproduce population statistics? Morstatter et al. (2013) could only ask
this with privileged firehose access; on Bluesky the census is free, so
anyone can replicate and extend their audit. *Data:* a multi-hour full
collection of posts, likes, and follows as ground truth. *Method:*
compute census quantities (hourly volumes, reply share, language
distribution, the like:post ratio) and compare each simulated sample's
estimates against them, mapping error as a function of sample design and
size. *Expected challenge:* the census window is large — plan storage as
aggregates-plus-features rather than raw events, and choose error
metrics that match how researchers would actually use the sample.

**3. Bot ecology from content-free signatures.** *Question:* what share
of accounts active in a window behave automatically, and what do
automated accounts spend their events on? *Data:* several hours of
stream events reduced to hashed DIDs, timestamps, collections, and
operations — no content needed. *Method:* per-account behavioral
features (inter-event timing regularity — automated accounts often act
at suspiciously exact intervals — round-the-clock activity without
diurnal dips, extreme like or follow rates), then clustering or anomaly
detection; validate against a hand-labeled set of self-disclosed bot
accounts, which Bluesky's norms make findable. *Expected challenge:*
there is no ground truth for *undisclosed* automation, so claims must
stay conservative and aggregate (Ferrara et al. 2016 review how hard the
labeling problem is) — and publicly naming specific accounts as bots is
an accusation, not a finding, so report ecosystem-level shares rather
than account lists.
